REP: Linda, thanks for making time. I'm hoping to learn how your front store is doing and whether there's a fit for our blood pressure monitor. Okay if I start with a few questions?
CUSTOMER: Sure, Daniel. I have about ten minutes.
REP: How much of your business comes from the front store these days?
CUSTOMER: Maybe twelve percent. It used to be twenty. The dollar store down the street took a lot of the basics. Toothpaste, shampoo, paper towels. We can't compete on price there, so I stopped trying.
REP: Which categories are still holding up for you?
CUSTOMER: Anything where people want advice. Diabetes supplies, compression socks, the vitamins I recommend. If I talk to someone about it, it sells. If it just sits on a shelf, the dollar store wins. Compression socks are a good example. They cost more than online, but I measure people, and they come back every three months.
REP: That's a great insight. Where do blood pressure monitors fall in that?
CUSTOMER: They should be an advice product, but they're not selling. I carry two models and I couldn't tell you the last time I sold one. Which is crazy, because probably a third of my regulars are on at least one blood pressure medication.
REP: What do you think is getting in the way?
CUSTOMER: Price, probably. And they're on the bottom shelf in aisle three where nobody sees them. Honestly, I put them there because they weren't selling, and now they really don't sell. It's a bit of a vicious circle.
REP: So the product needs to be near the conversation, and priced so that the conversation ends in a sale. The BP-200 retails at forty-four ninety-nine, your cost is twenty-two, and it comes with a small counter display so it sits right where you counsel.
CUSTOMER: Honestly, I don't know if my customers will trust a brand they've never heard of. They know the big names. Most of them are retirees, and they're loyal to brands they've used for thirty years.
REP: That's fair. Brand trust matters a lot with older customers. When a customer asks you which monitor to buy, what do you tell them today?
CUSTOMER: I tell them to get an upper-arm cuff, not a wrist one, and to make sure it's validated. Then I point at whatever's on the shelf. Which is a little embarrassing, because the shelf is the bottom of aisle three.
REP: Then the BP-200 checks your own boxes. It's an upper-arm cuff, it's clinically validated, and the validation certificate is printed on the box, so you can show it to the customer. Most of our pharmacists find that their recommendation matters more than the brand name. Would you be comfortable recommending it on that basis?
CUSTOMER: If it's validated, yes. My recommendation is what sells it anyway.
REP: Great. What would you need to see to give it a try?
CUSTOMER: A small first order. I'm not taking a pallet of anything.
REP: The minimum is one case of six, and the first order is sale-or-return for ninety days, so if it doesn't move you send it back for full credit. Would one case work?
CUSTOMER: One case is fine.
REP: Then let's do it. I'll place the order today so it ships with your Thursday wholesaler delivery, and I'll stop by Thursday the 1st at three to set up the counter display and leave a validation sheet for your staff. Does three work?
CUSTOMER: Three on Thursday works. Bring the sheet.
REP: Will do. Thanks, Linda.
CUSTOMER: Thank you.
